One general resurrection or two?
Does Scripture teach one resurrection of the just and unjust at Christ's return, or two bodily resurrections separated by the millennium?

Premillennialists read Revelation 20:4-6 as two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart. Amillennialists and postmillennialists, with the Reformed confessions, hold to a single general resurrection, appealing to John 5:28-29, Daniel 12:2 and Acts 24:15, and to Paul's tie between the resurrection and the destruction of death.

Revelation 20:4-6 describes two bodily resurrections separated by a thousand years: those who 'came to life and reigned with Christ' and 'the rest of the dead' who did not come to life until the thousand years ended. Paul's ordered resurrection, Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to him, 'then the end' (1 Corinthians 15:23-24), leaves room for an interval, and Luke 14:14 ('the resurrection of the righteous') and Philippians 3:11 (a resurrection 'out from among' the dead) hint at a resurrection of believers distinct from the general one. Ladd held that later revelation can disclose an interval earlier texts did not specify.

Jesus says 'an hour is coming' when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, the good to a resurrection of life and the evil to a resurrection of judgment (John 5:28-29); Daniel 12:2 and Acts 24:15 likewise speak of one resurrection of righteous and wicked together. Jesus repeatedly places the raising of believers 'on the last day' (John 6:39-40, 44, 54), and Matthew 25:31-46 sets the judgment of all nations at a single coming. Hoekema and Riddlebarger argue the clearer didactic texts should govern one highly symbolic vision.

Premillennialists reply that 'hour' (hora) in John need not be a single moment: the 'hour' that 'now is' in John 5:25 has lasted the whole church age, so the resurrection 'hour' of 5:28 can span a thousand years. Prophecy often compresses events later separated, as Isaiah 61:1-2 joins the two advents and Jesus stops reading mid-sentence (Luke 4:18-21). Some also read Daniel 12:2 as distinguishing 'some' raised to life from 'others' to shame.

Amillennialists answer that John 5:25 describes a spiritual raising and 5:28 a bodily one, so the elasticity of the first 'hour' cannot simply be transferred to the second. Believers are raised 'on the last day' (John 6:40) and unbelievers are judged 'on the last day' (John 12:48); placing a thousand years between them strains the phrase. They also note that the 'some... others' reading of Daniel 12:2 is a minority view among Hebrew scholars.

Postmillennialists such as Boettner and Gentry, with the Westminster Confession (32.3) and its catechisms, affirm one general resurrection of just and unjust at Christ's single return at the end of history. Paul's 'then comes the end' (1 Corinthians 15:24) follows directly on Christ's coming, Christ reigns now 'until' the last enemy, death, is destroyed (15:25-26), and death is swallowed up at the very resurrection of believers (15:54). That leaves no room for death to continue through a millennium after believers are raised.

Premillennialists argue that 'then' (eita) in 15:24 belongs to a sequence that already contains a long gap between Christ's resurrection and his coming (15:23), so a further interval between the coming and 'the end' fits Paul's wording. On this reading the reign 'until' all enemies are subdued (15:25) culminates in Christ's messianic kingdom on earth after the parousia.

Postmillennialists answer that the gap after the firstfruits is implied by Christ's ascension, whereas Paul gives no hint of a millennial gap. 15:54-55 ties the defeat of death to the resurrection at the last trumpet, so no death-bearing millennium can follow it. Gentry and Mathison also read the reign of 15:25 as Christ's present heavenly session (Psalm 110:1, Acts 2:34-36), already under way.
'They came to life' (ezesan) in Revelation 20:4-5
Is the 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:4-5 a bodily resurrection or the believer's present, spiritual life with Christ?

The same verb, ezesan, describes the saints who 'came to life' (20:4) and the rest of the dead who did not 'come to life' until the thousand years ended (20:5). Premillennialists insist both are bodily; amillennialists (and many postmillennialists) read the first as the soul's life with Christ in heaven or as regeneration, citing the 'first/second' contrast in Revelation.

Revelation 20:4 says the souls of the martyrs 'came to life' (ezesan) and reigned with Christ. Kline, Hoekema and Beale take this 'first resurrection' as the believer's entrance into heavenly life in the intermediate state. Kline argues that 'first' (protos) in Revelation marks the present, provisional order in contrast to the final one (21:1, 'the first heaven and the first earth had passed away'), so the first resurrection differs in kind from the bodily resurrection, just as the first (physical) death differs from the second death in the lake of fire (20:14).

Premillennialists since Henry Alford press a grammatical point: the same verb ezesan is used of the saints in 20:4 and of 'the rest of the dead' in 20:5. If the second is a bodily resurrection, consistency requires the first to be bodily too; reading one spiritually and the other literally in the same context, Alford argued, leaves language without fixed meaning. The same aorist describes Christ's bodily resurrection in Revelation 2:8 ('who died and came to life').

Kline and Hoekema reply that John himself signals a qualitative contrast with 'first' and 'second': the text names a first resurrection and a second death, implying a non-bodily first resurrection paired with a non-final first death. John 5:24-29 shows the same pattern, with the dead who 'hear and live' spiritually now and a bodily resurrection to come. The 20:5 statement is also negative ('did not come to life'), so the parallel is looser than claimed.

J. Ramsey Michaels, responding to Kline in the Westminster Theological Journal, accepted that 'first' can signal a difference in kind but argued it does not follow that the first resurrection is non-bodily. Premillennialists add that the 'souls of those beheaded' echoes Revelation 6:9-11, where the martyrs' souls wait for vindication; 20:4 grants that vindication by narrating a change of state, which is what resurrection means.

Dispensationalists such as Deere and Walvoord argue that 'resurrection' (anastasis, 20:5-6) almost everywhere in the New Testament means bodily resurrection. The martyrs' reward of reigning answers the promise to overcomers of authority over the nations (2:26-27) and the song that the redeemed 'will reign on the earth' (5:10). A purely heavenly intermediate state, they argue, does not fulfil a promise of reigning on the earth.

Beale replies that the saints' reign is already partly realised (Revelation 1:6, 'he made us a kingdom') and that the intermediate state is participation in Christ's present heavenly reign (Ephesians 2:6). 'Resurrection' in 20:5-6 is qualified by 'first', marking it as distinct, and the thrones of 20:4, like the thrones elsewhere in Revelation, are in heaven.

Premillennialists respond that Ephesians 2:6 describes the living believer's positional union with Christ, not the post-mortem reward given specifically to martyrs, and that John's sequence (souls of the beheaded, then they 'came to life') narrates an event at a point in time. They regard the amillennial reading as importing categories from elsewhere into an otherwise natural sequence.
The binding of Satan: now or future?
Was Satan bound at Christ's first coming, or does Revelation 20:1-3 describe a future, total confinement?

Amillennialists and postmillennialists hold that Satan was bound at the first advent so that he can no longer prevent the gospel from reaching the nations. Premillennialists argue that the language of Revelation 20:1-3 describes a complete removal from earthly activity that has not yet happened.

Amillennialists (Riddlebarger, Hoekema, Storms), with postmillennialists, hold that Satan was bound at Christ's first coming. Jesus described his exorcisms as binding the strong man in order to plunder his house (Matthew 12:28-29, using the same verb deo as Revelation 20:2), saw Satan fall like lightning (Luke 10:18), and announced that the ruler of this world would be cast out as he drew all people to himself (John 12:31-32). The binding in Revelation 20:3 has a specific purpose: Satan can no longer deceive the nations as before (Acts 14:16, Acts 17:30), so the gospel goes to the Gentiles.

Premillennialists argue the binding of Revelation 20 is far more than a restriction: Satan is seized, chained, thrown into the abyss, which is then shut and sealed over him (20:1-3). Yet the New Testament describes Satan in the church age as prowling like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), blinding unbelievers' minds (2 Corinthians 4:4) and at work in the disobedient (Ephesians 2:2). Waymeyer concludes that a partial, present restraint does not match the totality of John's language.

Amillennialists respond that apocalyptic imagery depicts spiritual realities; the chain and the abyss are no more literal than the dragon himself. The binding has one stated purpose, 'so that he might not deceive the nations', and does not claim to end all satanic activity, just as a dog on a long chain is restrained without being idle. The worldwide spread of the gospel since Pentecost (Matthew 28:18-20) is the evidence of this restriction.

Premillennialists reply that 2 Corinthians 4:4, Revelation 12:9 and 13:14 describe Satan's present work precisely as deception, including of 'the whole world', the very activity 20:3 says is halted. They also argue that the strong-man saying concerns Jesus' authority over demons in his ministry, not a sealed confinement lasting through the church age.

Historic premillennialists such as Ladd grant that Christ won a decisive victory over Satan at the cross, but argue that Revelation 20 depicts a further stage. Revelation 12 portrays Satan thrown down to the earth in great wrath (12:12); 20:1-3 portrays him removed from the earth altogether. Because these are distinct events in John's sequence, the first-advent victory texts do not exhaust 20:1-3.

Postmillennialists such as Gentry, agreeing with amillennialists on timing, note that Revelation 12 ties Satan's fall to Christ's ascension and to the saints' victory 'by the blood of the Lamb' (12:5, 12:10-11), the same first-advent setting. His raging and his inability to deceive the nations are complementary perspectives on one defeat, and the ongoing discipling of the nations (Matthew 28:19) shows the binding at work in history.

Premillennialists answer that the two visions differ in location (earth versus abyss) and effect (raging versus sealed), so one cannot easily be read as the other. They also note that Paul and John describe the present age as marked by deception (2 Thessalonians 2:9-11, 1 John 5:19), which is hard to square with nations no longer deceived.
Matthew 13: kingdom growth or wheat and tares until the end?
Do the kingdom parables of Matthew 13 forecast the gospel's progressive worldwide dominance, or a mixed growth of good and evil until the harvest?

Postmillennialists read the mustard seed and leaven as pictures of the kingdom's eventual pervasive triumph in history. Amillennialists stress the wheat and tares growing together until the end of the age; some dispensationalists read the parables as describing a mixed or even corrupted professing church.

Postmillennialists read the kingdom parables of Matthew 13 as forecasting the gospel's progressive, worldwide growth before Christ returns. The mustard seed grows from the smallest of seeds into a tree in which the birds nest (13:31-32), echoing Daniel 4 and Ezekiel 17's image of a great kingdom sheltering the nations, and the leaven works until 'all' the dough is leavened (13:33). Read with Daniel's stone that becomes a mountain filling the whole earth (Daniel 2:35, 44), Boettner, Mathison and Gentry see a pattern of gradual, pervasive kingdom triumph within history.

Amillennialists point to the parable of the wheat and the tares in the same chapter: good and evil grow together 'until the harvest', which is 'the end of the age' (13:30, 13:39-40), and the dragnet likewise gathers good and bad until the end (13:47-50). Riddlebarger and Hoekema argue this describes parallel development of good and evil throughout the age, and that the mustard seed and leaven teach the kingdom's unexpected reach and hidden power rather than a Christianised world.

Postmillennialists reply that the tares parable teaches coexistence, not proportion. The field is the world, and the point is that the servants must not uproot the tares by force but leave separation to the final judgment; nothing says the tares stay as numerous as the wheat. Boettner and Gentry argue that evil persisting until the end is fully compatible with the gospel becoming dominant, as weeds can remain in a field that yields an overwhelming wheat harvest.

Amillennialists respond that the parable's emphasis on both growing to the harvest, combined with warnings of increasing lawlessness and a final apostasy (Matthew 24:12, 2 Thessalonians 2:3), makes a closing golden age hard to see. Hoekema proposes a 'realistic optimism': Christ reigns and his kingdom grows now, but conflict and suffering continue until the consummation.

Many classic dispensationalists read Matthew 13 as the 'mysteries of the kingdom' in the interadvent age, which Pentecost characterised as a mixed sphere of Christian profession. Leaven is elsewhere almost always a symbol of corruption (Matthew 16:6, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8), so it may depict false teaching spreading in Christendom, and the birds lodging in the mustard tree may recall the birds that snatch the seed (13:4, 13:19). On this reading the parables forecast a corrupted professing church, not global conversion.

Postmillennialists, with most commentators, respond that the parable says 'the kingdom of heaven is like leaven', so the leaven is the kingdom itself and cannot here symbolise evil. Leavened loaves were offered to God at the feast of firstfruits (Leviticus 23:17), and a tree sheltering birds is a recognised image of a great kingdom over the nations (Daniel 4:12, Ezekiel 31:6).

Many dispensationalists, especially progressive ones, accept the positive reading of the leaven but argue the parables describe the extent of the kingdom's present form, not worldwide righteousness, and that the kingdom in its full Davidic sense awaits the King's return (Luke 19:11-15, Acts 1:6-7). The core disagreement is therefore about when the kingdom is consummated, not these images alone.
'Perilous times' (2 Timothy 3) and postmillennial hope
Does Paul's warning about 'difficult times in the last days' describe the whole church age, ruling out a future Christianised world?

Amillennialists and premillennialists often cite 2 Timothy 3 as a portrait of the entire last days. Postmillennialists, notably Gentry in reply to James White, read it as an occasional warning about specific false teachers whose progress Paul says will be checked; partial preterists add that the 'last days' are often the closing decades of the old covenant era.

Paul warns that 'in the last days difficult (chalepoi) times will come', listing people who are lovers of self, money and pleasure, holding a form of godliness while denying its power (2 Timothy 3:1-5). He adds that all who desire to live godly lives will be persecuted and that evil people and impostors 'will go on from bad to worse' (3:12-13). Since the last days span the whole age from Christ's first coming (Hebrews 1:2), amillennialists (and premillennialists) argue this characterises the entire church age, which sits uneasily with an expected Christianised world; James White has pressed this point in debate with postmillennialists.

Gentry answers that 2 Timothy is an occasional letter addressing Timothy's own situation: Paul tells Timothy to 'avoid such people' (3:5), describes those who are already creeping into households (3:6) and compares them to Jannes and Jambres. Crucially, Paul says such men 'will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all' (3:9). Iain Murray likewise read the passage as warning about the contagion of contemporary false teachers, not forecasting inevitable decline across the age.

Amillennialists reply that a letter can be occasional and still describe recurring features of the last days; the present-tense commands show those days had begun, not that they would end. Paul's statement that 'all who desire to live a godly life will be persecuted' (3:12) reads as a principle for the whole age, consistent with Jesus' warnings (John 15:18-20) and Paul's own teaching that we enter the kingdom through many tribulations (Acts 14:22).

Postmillennialists agree persecution recurs but distinguish recurring periods of moral decline from a uniform downward trajectory. The 'bad to worse' of 3:13 describes the impostors' own spiral, which Paul has just said will be checked (3:9). Since the last days span the whole age, even amillennialists must allow that they include seasons of revival and reformation, which shows the text is not a forecast of the age's overall direction.

Partial preterists such as DeMar add that New Testament 'last days' language often refers to the final days of the old covenant order before AD 70 (compare 1 Corinthians 10:11, 1 Peter 4:7). The vices of 2 Timothy 3 and the apostasy described in Jude and 2 Peter fit the turbulent decades before Jerusalem's fall, so the passage describes a period already past rather than the church's permanent condition.

Amillennialists respond that the New Testament's last days are the age between the comings, not just the decades before AD 70; Acts 2:17 and Hebrews 9:26 present them as the eschatological era Christ inaugurated, which runs to his return. Confining 2 Timothy 3 to the pre-70 decades would also limit its function as instruction for later churches in a way the letter itself does not suggest (3:16-17).

Preterists answer that they do not deny the passage's application to later believers, only its use as a prophecy of the age's long-term trajectory. They read 'the end of the ages' (Hebrews 9:26) and 'on whom the end of the ages has come' (1 Corinthians 10:11) as transitional texts focused on the passing of the old covenant order.
The church and Israel: distinct peoples or one?
Is the church a distinct people alongside a national Israel with its own future promises, or the one people of God in which Israel's promises are fulfilled?

Dispensationalists maintain a distinction between Israel and the church; covenant theologians see one people of God across the covenants; progressive covenantalists see Christ as the true Israel and the church as the new covenant people in him. Many in all camps, including Puritan postmillennialists, expect a future large-scale conversion of Jewish people from Romans 11.

Dispensationalists hold that the church and Israel are distinct peoples within God's single redemptive purpose. Paul says Israel according to the flesh still has the covenants and promises (Romans 9:4-5), distinguishes 'Jews, Greeks and the church of God' (1 Corinthians 10:32), and foresees the salvation of 'all Israel' after the fullness of the Gentiles, because God's gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:25-29). Vlach argues the church is a new entity begun at Pentecost (Matthew 16:18, Ephesians 3:5-6) and that unconditional national and land promises (Genesis 12:1-3, Jeremiah 31:35-37) remain for ethnic Israel.

Covenant theologians argue for one people of God across the covenants. Gentiles are grafted into the one olive tree (Romans 11:17-24), the dividing wall is broken down to make 'one new man' (Ephesians 2:14-16), those in Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29), and Paul can bless 'the Israel of God' (Galatians 6:16), which many take as the whole church. The church is therefore the continuation and fulfilment of Israel, centred on the Messiah as the true Israel.

Dispensationalists respond that the olive tree represents covenant blessing rather than Israel's identity, and in Romans 11 the natural branches are explicitly ethnic Israel, whose regrafting is future. 'One new man' unites Jew and Gentile in salvation without erasing ethnic distinctions, just as male and female remain in Galatians 3:28. They read Galatians 6:16 ('and upon the Israel of God') as referring to believing Jews, a reading defended by scholars such as S. Lewis Johnson.

Covenant theologians note that many of them also expect a future mass conversion of ethnic Jews from Romans 11, a hallmark of Puritan postmillennialism traced by Iain Murray. The dispute, then, is not Israel's future salvation but whether it comes as a separate programme with distinct land and temple promises; they argue the New Testament instead extends the inheritance to the whole world (Romans 4:13).

Progressive covenantalists (Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum) reject both 'replacement' and a permanent Israel-church distinction: Christ is the true Israel, and the church is the new covenant people in union with him. The new covenant was promised to the house of Israel (Jeremiah 31:31-34) yet is inaugurated for the church (Luke 22:20, Hebrews 8:8-13), showing that Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared by all who are in him.

Progressive dispensationalists such as Blaising and Bock agree that the church shares in the new covenant now, but call this an initial, partial fulfilment; its national dimensions, a regathered and restored Israel (Ezekiel 36:24-28), await Christ's return. Gentile inclusion in new covenant blessings, they argue, does not require Israel's distinct promises to lapse.

Wellum responds that typological fulfilment in Christ is not a 'partial' fulfilment awaiting a second national stage: the land is itself a type of the new creation, and Hebrews says the patriarchs sought a better, heavenly country (Hebrews 11:16). The burden, he argues, lies on those who posit a restored national programme to show it from New Testament texts.
The timing of the rapture
Will the church be caught up before the tribulation, during it (before God's wrath), or at Christ's single return after it?

Within futurist premillennialism, pretribulationists place the rapture before Daniel's seventieth week, prewrath advocates place it within the second half before the day of the Lord's wrath, and posttribulationists identify it with the visible return after the tribulation. Amillennialists and postmillennialists generally read 1 Thessalonians 4 as describing Christ's single return, close to the posttribulational reading.

Pretribulationists hold that Christ will take the church to himself (John 14:1-3, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18) before the seven-year tribulation of Daniel's seventieth week. Believers are 'not destined for wrath' (1 Thessalonians 5:9) and are promised to be kept 'from the hour of trial' coming on the whole world (Revelation 3:10). The rapture is imminent and preceded by no signs (Titus 2:13), whereas the coming to earth follows clear signs, implying two stages; and Walvoord and Ryrie note that the church (ekklesia) is not mentioned on earth in Revelation 4-18.

Posttribulationists (Gundry, Ladd, Moo) argue Scripture describes one return. The elect are gathered 'immediately after the tribulation' (Matthew 24:29-31) at the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52), and Paul tells the Thessalonians the day of the Lord will not come until the apostasy and the man of lawlessness appear (2 Thessalonians 2:1-4). The 'meeting' (apantesis) of 1 Thessalonians 4:17 normally describes going out to welcome a visiting dignitary and escorting him back. Gundry notes that no text places the rapture before the tribulation, while several place Christ's coming and the resurrection after it.

Pretribulationists answer that the Olivet discourse addresses Israel, so its 'elect' are tribulation saints; the 'last trumpet' of 1 Corinthians 15 is not the seventh trumpet judgment of Revelation; and 2 Thessalonians 2 reassures believers that they are not in the day of the Lord, which would be a strange comfort if they expected to endure it. Ryrie, reviewing Gundry, argued that the imminence passages are hard to reconcile with a return preceded by identifiable tribulation events.

Posttribulationists respond that the Olivet discourse addresses the disciples, the church's founders, whom Jesus also commissions with his presence 'to the end of the age' (Matthew 28:20). New Testament imminence, they argue, means expectancy and readiness, not that no prophesied event can precede the return; Paul himself names events that must come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

Prewrath advocates (Rosenthal, Kurschner) agree that the church is delivered before God's wrath but deny that the whole seventieth week is wrath. They distinguish the 'great tribulation', the Antichrist's persecution of the saints (Matthew 24:21-22, Revelation 13:7), from the day of the Lord's wrath, which is announced only after the cosmic signs of the sixth seal ('the great day of their wrath has come', Revelation 6:16-17). The rapture therefore occurs in the second half of the week, after the Antichrist is revealed but before the trumpet and bowl judgments.

Pretribulationists reply that the Lamb himself opens every seal (Revelation 6:1), so the judgments from the first seal onward are divine, and 'the wrath of the Lamb' in 6:16 can describe wrath already under way. They also argue that Daniel's seventieth week is a unit directed at Daniel's people and city (Daniel 9:24), so the church's removal belongs before it begins.

Prewrath writers answer that the aorist 'has come' (elthen) in 6:17 announces wrath arriving at that point, and that the Lamb's opening of the seals no more makes them wrath than God's sovereignty makes all suffering wrath. They also note that Jesus' own order (tribulation cut short, cosmic signs, gathering of the elect; Matthew 24:22, 29-31) matches Revelation 6-7, where a great multitude 'coming out of the great tribulation' appears in heaven right after the sixth seal (7:9-14).
The early Fathers, chiliasm and Augustine
Was premillennialism (chiliasm) the consensus of the earliest church, displaced only later by Augustine?

Chiliasm is clearly attested in Papias, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and Tertullian. Premillennialists see it as the earliest view; Charles Hill and other amillennialists argue a non-chiliast stream was equally early; Augustine's City of God XX shaped Western exegesis for a millennium. All sides agree Scripture, not the Fathers, is decisive.

Historic premillennialists point out that chiliasm, belief in an earthly thousand-year kingdom after Christ's return, is the earliest clearly attested millennial view. Papias (reported by Irenaeus and Eusebius), Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 80-81), Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.32-36) and Tertullian taught it, and Irenaeus traced it to elders who had known John. Opposition came later, chiefly from Alexandrian allegorists such as Origen, and was consolidated by Augustine's City of God XX, so premillennialists see their view as a recovery of the early church's hope.

Charles Hill's Regnum Caelorum argues that a non-chiliast stream was early and widespread, visible in writers such as Clement of Rome, Polycarp, Ignatius and the Epistle to Diognetus. Justin himself concedes that many Christians 'of pure and godly' mind did not share his view (Dialogue 80). Hill links chiliasm to the belief that souls wait in an underworld until the resurrection; those who expected to be with Christ in heaven at death (Philippians 1:23, 2 Corinthians 5:8) had no need of an earthly interim kingdom, so there were two coherent early patterns, not one consensus.

Brian Collins, evaluating Hill in Bibliotheca Sacra, argues that the claimed link between chiliasm and an underworld intermediate state fails: Irenaeus taught a millennium while also allowing a heavenly intermediate state. Many of Hill's non-chiliast witnesses are arguments from silence, whereas the chiliast witnesses are explicit. Some premillennialists also read Justin's concession as less sweeping than Hill does, since he immediately condemns those who deny the resurrection of the flesh.

Defenders of Hill reply that Dialogue 80 distinguishes godly Christians who disagree from the heretics Justin then condemns, and that silence across several early writers who do discuss the end is significant. They add that later amillennialism did not need Augustine to invent it: Augustine had himself once held a chiliast view and changed his mind on exegetical grounds that he sets out in City of God XX.

Postmillennialists (and others) argue that early prevalence is not decisive. Second-century chiliasm was often bound up with material expectations, such as Papias' description of fantastically fruitful vines, that modern premillennialists do not adopt, and doctrine rests on Scripture rather than early consensus. Augustine's reading of Revelation 20 as Christ's present reign shaped Western exegesis for a millennium, and, as Iain Murray argues, the Puritan hope of gospel advance grew from that Augustinian framework.

Premillennialists agree Scripture is decisive, but argue that the earliest interpreters, nearest to John's language and world, read Revelation 20 sequentially, which counts against claims that a premillennial reading is a modern novelty. They also distinguish historic premillennialism from both crude chiliasm and modern dispensationalism, so criticisms of second-century excesses do not touch Ladd's version.

Postmillennialists respond that proximity cuts both ways: the same early writers also held views, such as a fixed six-thousand-year world-week, that few modern premillennialists follow, and Eusebius already judged Papias limited in understanding on these matters. They suggest the historical claim be stated modestly: chiliasm was prominent in the second century but not unanimous.
